The lecture on **isolation forests** was covered on **2026-11-06** in the **School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning** course.

Key points from that lecture:
- The topic was anomaly detection, with isolation forest being the main focus
- Anomalies are isolated in fewer splits (the key definition)
- The professor set contamination to 0.05 in the demo, flagging the top 5% of points as anomalies
- Students were assigned to read the chapter and try the homework problem on isolation forest

Sources: [[Research/Isolation Forest]], [[School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning/Lectures - CSCI 470]]

Passages: [[School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning/Lectures - CSCI 470#^c1crdtw|Lectures - CSCI 470 › 2026-11-06]], [[School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning/Lectures - CSCI 470#^t21-29|Lectures - CSCI 470 › 21:29]], [[School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning/Lectures - CSCI 470#^t39-55|Lectures - CSCI 470 › 39:55]]

In the lecture on November 6th, at **21:29**, the professor said:

> "In the demo I set contamination to 0.05, so the model flags the top five percent of points as anomalies. Set it too high and you start flagging normal data."

So the key point is that contamination controls the false positive rate — if set too high, the isolation forest will incorrectly flag normal data points as anomalies.

Sources: [[School/CSCI 470 - Machine Learning/Lectures - CSCI 470]]
